title: How maps lie
text: Every map {{1}} three problems at once: projection, scale and selection. Flatten the round Earth onto a sheet of paper and something must {{2}} way. Gerardus Mercator's sixteenth-century compromise {{3}} navigators handsomely for four centuries, but at a price: on his grid, Greenland balloons {{4}} beyond its true size, while Africa, which could hold it fourteen times over, shrinks towards insignificance. The celebrated London Underground map goes further and {{5}} geography altogether in favour of clarity. It shows {{6}} passengers actually need — which line, which change, how many stops — and generations of tourists have been astonished by the real distances their journeys covered underground. Maps of elections {{7}} the same trick: vast, sparsely inhabited regions glow in triumphant colour while crowded cities shrink to specks, and viewers unfamiliar with the manipulation misread landslides where none occurred. None of this is dishonesty, exactly; every map must leave something out, because everything cannot be true at once. But it does mean that a map is an {{8}} about the world rather than a window onto it — and the careful reader learns to ask who drew it, for whom, and what was left behind.

gaps.explanation: 'juggles three problems at once' — keeps many things in play.
'something must give way' — yield under pressure.
'served navigators handsomely' — worked well for them.
'balloons vastly beyond its true size' — by a huge amount.
'sacrifices geography in favour of clarity' — gives one thing up for another.
'shows what passengers need' — nominal relative pronoun.
'pull the same trick' — do the same clever deed (fixed phrase).
'a map is an argument about the world' — it takes a position.
